ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 15
note: Augustine's treatment of the Samaritan-woman scene reads Christ's living water as spiritual grace rather than ordinary well water alone. It shows how a Christian interpreter changes the literal traveller-and-well meeting that parallels the commentary.
The commentary distinguishes the path of those favored by God from the paths of wrath and straying; the Didache opens its instruction with two ways, one of life and one of death.

The Didache prefers baptism in living water. Its ritual preference turns running or fresh water into a sign of new life, extending the commentary's literal contrast between a life-giving source and lost water.

basis: way of light and way of darkness
note: The commentary asks for the straight path rather than the paths of wrath and straying; Barnabas sets out a way of light against a way of darkness, a Christian ethical expansion of the two-way contrast.

Origen's homily on Isaac's reopened wells treats digging wells as recovering the deep waters of Scripture. The reading gives a Christian interpretive afterlife to the commentary's well as a source that must be reached and kept open.

The commentary labels al-ʿālamīn from ʿ-L-M and also develops a deep, water-filled well from that family; the Peshitta uses cognate ʿālmā for “world,” showing the word’s spatial world sense in a Christian text.

In the usual chapter division, Mary goes out with a water jar and hears the annunciatory greeting. This Christian apocryphal well-side encounter belongs beside the commentary's women at water, where drawing water becomes a setting for divine gift.

The commentary brings cloud, travel, and water together; Paul recalls Israel’s ancestors under the cloud and on their wilderness passage, supplying the Christian pilgrimage setting for his water reference.
Israel's wilderness journey takes place under the cloud. Together with the water in verse 4, this creates a Christian rereading in which cloud and water accompany a people on the way.

The commentary treats water as the literal support of the traveler; Paul rereads Israel’s wilderness drink from the rock as spiritual drink from Christ, adding a Christian interpretation to water on the journey.

basis: water from the rock on the way
note: The commentary says water keeps a traveler’s work standing; Paul recalls Israel drinking from a spiritual rock in the wilderness, making provision on a journey the basis for a Christian reading.

basis: water from the rock for the journey
note: The wilderness people drink from the spiritual rock that follows them. It is a strong counterpart to the commentary's claim that water beside the traveller sustains the journey and its affairs.
The commentary connects rain-soaked soil, plant growth, and the raising of the dead; Paul says the seed is not made alive unless it dies, using planted growth to explain resurrection.

basis: a bare kernel becomes a plant
note: The commentary says rain leaves a green trace on earth; Paul distinguishes the bare kernel sown from the body that will grow, making plant emergence a model for resurrection.
The commentary links renewed earth to the resurrection of the dead; Paul explicitly compares a perishable seed sown in the ground with the imperishable body raised.
Paul plants, Apollos waters, and God gives the growth. Its agricultural distinction makes explicit the commentary's basic figure: water serves growth, yet the giver of growth remains God.
Human flesh is compared to grass that withers and a flower that falls. As an explicit inverse, it helps define the significance of the commentary's exceptional plant that does not wither in summer.

basis: springs without water and driven mist
note: The false teachers are compared to waterless springs and mists driven by storm. Its paired failures of well and cloud form a precise inverse to the commentary's full well and productive cloud.
God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness. It exactly connects divine rain with the food and livelihood results developed in the commentary.

basis: a fixed day to judge the world
note: The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Paul says God appointed a day to judge the inhabited world in righteousness and gave assurance by raising the appointed man.
On a wilderness road the Ethiopian traveller sees water and asks for baptism. The scene is a Christian travel-and-water meeting that gives the commentary's road beside water a ritual extension.

basis: land drinks rain and yields plants
note: Land that drinks repeatedly falling rain and produces useful vegetation receives blessing. It directly restates the commentary's heavenly water making the earth grow.

basis: farmer waits for early and late rain
note: The farmer waits for the earth's precious fruit through the early and late rains. It offers a New Testament seasonal analogue to the commentary's first rain and rain-grown vegetation.
The commentary asks to be guided on the straight path; John the Baptist identifies himself with Isaiah’s voice calling for the Lord’s way to be made straight.

The commentary calls the plant-growing cloud by the Qur’anic title Rabb; John preserves the Aramaic address rabbi and glosses it as teacher, showing a related Semitic master-title in a human teaching relation.

basis: ordinary well water becomes living water
note: The commentary insists that a traveler’s water sustains his affairs; Jesus interprets the well encounter through the gift of living water, adding a spiritual reading to literal thirst.

basis: gift of God and living water
note: Jesus offers living water at the well. It moves the commentary's full, beneficial well from physical support to a divine gift without erasing the scene of drawing water.
The commentary follows rain and well water into enduring life; Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring within the recipient, a Christian expansion from provision to lasting life.
The water Jesus gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. Its self-renewing spring is a concentrated Christian analogue to the commentary's water that keeps life and affairs standing.

basis: weary traveler rests at a well
note: The commentary’s Musa reaches a well after travel and later withdraws to shade; Jesus, tired from his journey, sits beside Jacob’s well, a close Christian well-side travel scene.

basis: weary traveller seated at Jacob's well
note: Jesus, wearied by travel, sits at Jacob's well. This makes a close well-side counterpart to the commentary's traveller who reaches water and whose journey depends on it.

basis: request for water at the well
note: The commentary has Musa water women at Midian; Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink at Jacob’s well, making the well encounter turn on who gives water.
A woman arrives to draw water, turning the well into a meeting between a traveller and a woman obtaining water. It closely accompanies the commentary's Musa, the two women, and the Midian water.

The sick man says that when the pool's water is stirred, he has no one to put him in it before another enters. It supplies a Christian scene where need, water, and the absence of a helper meet, a useful counterpart to the women who cannot water without aid.

basis: thirsty people are invited to come
note: The commentary says water keeps the traveler from thirst and supports life; Jesus invites the thirsty to come and drink, turning thirst into a direct spiritual appeal.
The commentary traces water from source to soil and growth; Jesus describes rivers of living water flowing from the believer, extending the image from provision to inward abundance.

The believer is described as the source from whom streams of living water flow. It extends the living-water image from the well to an overflowing source, a useful counterpart to the commentary's abundant gathered water.

Jude's false teachers are waterless clouds carried by winds. This is a deliberate negative inversion of the commentary's moist, rain-bearing cloud that grows plants: a cloud that promises but gives no life.

basis: feet guided into the way of peace
note: The commentary asks God to guide “us” on a straight path; Zechariah’s hymn says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace.
The commentary moves from invoking God’s name to divine rule and guidance; Luke’s Lord’s Prayer likewise begins with the Father’s name and kingdom before its requests.
The commentary follows rainwater into food and livelihood; Luke’s prayer asks for daily bread, placing provision within the same petitionary form.
The commentary asks to be guided away from a mistaken path; Luke’s prayer asks not to be brought into trial, a specific prayer for protection from a wrong course.

basis: leading ox or donkey to water
note: Jesus invokes the ordinary act of untying an ox or donkey and leading it to water. The concrete animal-watering practice complements the commentary's water as livelihood and its well scene of flocks needing to be watered.
The commentary’s sirat is a road to be made straight; Luke quotes Isaiah’s command to prepare the Lord’s way and make his paths straight.
The commentary asks for guidance on a straight path; Mark opens John’s wilderness preaching with Isaiah’s call to prepare the Lord’s way.
The commentary names the Owner of the Day of Judgment and separates the favored from the rejected; Jesus depicts the Son of Man enthroned and gathering the nations for judgment.
The commentary asks for the path of those granted favor rather than those under wrath; the king calls the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them.
The commentary distinguishes the favored from those under anger; the same judgment scene sends the cursed away, giving a concrete Christian counterpart to its divided outcome.
The commentary asks for the straight path; Matthew applies Isaiah’s wilderness voice to John, who prepares the Lord’s way and makes his paths straight.

basis: rain falls on just and unjust
note: The commentary says rain corrects people’s condition and benefits them while the surah distinguishes favored from rejected paths; Jesus says God gives rain to both just and unjust, making rain’s reach broader than the moral division.
The Father sends rain on both just and unjust. It gives a New Testament articulation of rain as unearned divine beneficence, relevant to the commentary's rain as mercy and benefit.
The commentary calls God master of the Judgment Day; the Lord’s Prayer petitions for God’s kingdom and will, placing divine rule before requests for provision and guidance.
The commentary moves from rain and water to food for people and animals; the Lord’s Prayer asks for daily bread, making sustenance part of the prayer’s petition.

basis: lead away from trial and evil
note: The commentary asks for the right path and exclusion from straying; the Lord’s Prayer asks not to be led into trial and to be delivered from evil, a neighboring petition for safe direction.
The commentary opens with bism and develops its name/mark association; the Lord’s Prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, a parallel invocation before petitions.
The commentary asks for the straight path and excludes the astray; Jesus contrasts the narrow gate and hard way leading to life with the broad way leading to destruction.
The commentary asks to be guided on the straight road; Jesus says the way to life is narrow and difficult and few find it.

basis: shut sky so rain does not fall
note: The witnesses have authority to shut the sky so that rain does not fall during their prophecy. Its withheld-rain image is a specific inverse to the commentary's cloud and rain as mercy that restores life.
The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Revelation depicts the dead standing before the throne and being judged from the opened books according to their deeds.
The thirsty receive water of life freely from the spring. It gives an eschatological form to the commentary's water as indispensable gift and remedy for need.
The commentary calls water the support and “king” of human affairs; Revelation’s river of life flows from the throne of God and the Lamb, joining rule to life-giving water.

A bright river of water of life proceeds from God's throne. The throne-source relationship gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's unusual claim that water is a kingdom's or traveller's holding power.
The commentary links gathered water to persistent vegetation; Revelation places the tree of life beside the river, bearing fruit and leaves for healing.

The trees beside the life-river bear fruit continually and their leaves serve healing. Its flourishing trees supply a Christian counterpart to the commentary's plant nourished into unfading freshness.

basis: guide to springs of living water
note: The commentary joins guidance on a road to water for the traveler; the Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water.
The Lamb shepherds and guides the thirsty to springs of the water of life. It closely meets the commentary's way, guidance, shepherding provision, and water that removes want.
The commentary develops rain as a mark on the earth and distinguishes people on the final path; Revelation seals God’s servants before harm comes to earth, sea, and trees.

The waters become bitter and people die from them. This is a specific negative counterpart to the commentary's sweet, abundant, life-sustaining water and to its image of water repairing rather than harming a community.

Hermas's vision of the Church as a tower built on water explains water as the means through which life is saved. This early Christian interpretation turns water into an actual foundation, closely echoing the commentary's qiwām and milāk language for what keeps a matter standing.

On Genesis 37:24, the Talmud reads "no water" as leaving room for snakes and scorpions. The interpretation sharpens the commentary's Joseph contrast: the biblical pit is not a usable water source even when it is not simply empty space.

The Honi story treats drought-ending rain as a communal need and distinguishes an unhelpful rain from the desired beneficial rain. It gives a Jewish narrative counterpart to the commentary's rain that repairs a people's condition.

The Talmud develops the scriptural comparison of Torah with water. This changes water from material provision into descending and sought instruction, a useful interpretive bridge to the commentary's pairing of guidance with sustaining water.

basis: clouds of glory and Miriam's well
note: The Talmud associates Israel's wilderness gifts with the cloud and Miriam's well. Its deliberate pairing is an especially close Jewish counterpart to this section's meeting of growing cloud and well.

basis: prayer formula for wind and rain
note: The commentary joins wind, clouds, and rain; the Talmud explains the seasonal prayer formula that asks God to make wind blow and rain fall.

basis: rain and resurrection as divine acts
note: The commentary cites a Qur’anic scene where rain-bearing clouds lead into the raising of the dead; the Talmud groups rain and resurrection among powers God has not delegated, giving the same pair a Jewish theological frame.

The commentary distinguishes the path of those favored from the paths of wrath and straying; the Community Rule contrasts the spirits of truth and perversity and their opposed ways, giving a Jewish sectarian account of moral paths.

basis: Adam recognizes need of rain and prays
note: In the usual division, the midrash explains the delayed rain of Genesis 2 by saying that rain came after Adam recognized its need and prayed. It adds a Jewish reading in which rain, vegetation, human need, and prayer are deliberately joined.

The tradition commonly cited at this place has the well water rise for Rebekah as she draws for the camels. It re-reads the traveller-and-well service of Genesis 24 as a sign of blessing, adding a Jewish interpretive layer to the commentary's water as benefit.

The common division of Genesis Rabbah says that the water rose to meet Jacob at Haran. That interpretive expansion transforms the covered well of Genesis 29 into a responsive source, useful beside the commentary's well apparatus and abundant water.

The Mishnah lists Miriam's well among things prepared at creation's twilight. This later Jewish tradition makes a well a providential provision for Israel, clarifying the commentary's water as what sustains a travelling community.

basis: well enclosures for pilgrims and animals
note: The Mishnah permits a distinctive post-and-enclosure arrangement around wells so that festival travellers' animals can be watered. Its legal concern with well-side construction, travellers, and animal water is unusually close to the commentary's detailed well-mouth apparatus.

The Mishnah fixes when a community begins mentioning and requesting rain. Its concrete liturgical ordering of rain gives a Jewish communal counterpart to the commentary's rain as mercy and repair rather than merely weather.
The commentary places rain, harvest, and the Day of Judgment together; the Mishnah says the world is judged at Sukkot concerning water, joining seasonal rain to a global judgment calendar.

basis: water drawing as a temple rite
note: The commentary describes water drawn from a well and rain as divine provision; the Mishnah describes drawing water from Siloam for the Temple’s water libation, making water-drawing a liturgical act.

basis: seasonal mention of rain in prayer
note: The commentary develops rain and wind as divine provision; the Mishnah debates when the rain petition enters the daily prayer cycle, showing rain as a recurring Jewish liturgical request.
The commentary calls water the support of affairs and traces it into food; Sirach lists water among the necessities of human life beside bread, fire, salt, and other provisions.
The commentary follows wind-borne clouds until they become heavy with rain; Elijah’s servant sees a small cloud rising from the sea as the sign of coming rain.
Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rise from the sea before the rain. It is a focused companion to the commentary's cloud that forms above and becomes the bearer of growing water.
The commentary makes wind and cloud the forerunners of rain; in Elijah’s scene the sky darkens with clouds and wind before a great rain falls.
The sky turns dark with clouds and wind before a great rain. Its linked weather actors answer the commentary's prolonged cloud and moist south-wind scene without requiring the same wind direction.

Elisha throws salt into a spring and declares its waters healed, so that death and barrenness will no longer come from it. It gives a sharp biblical counterpart to rain or water improving a people's condition and to the commentary's fresh, beneficial water.

The valley will be filled with water even though neither wind nor rain is seen. Its explicit separation of water provision from visible wind and rain is a useful contrary configuration beside the commentary's wind moving cloud toward rain.

basis: a king longs for well water
note: The commentary says a tribe calls its waters “our kings” because water holds affairs together; David, himself king, longs for a drink from the well of Bethlehem.

David longs for water from the well by Bethlehem's gate. The king's desire for a particular well makes water a royal concern, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary's phrase that a community's waters are its kings.

basis: men risk their lives to draw water
note: The commentary says the traveler’s water lets him hold his affairs in hand; David’s men break through enemy lines to draw the well water he longs for.

basis: men draw and carry well water to David
note: David's warriors break through, draw water from the Bethlehem well, and bring it to him. The verse supplies the physical act of drawing and carrying water for a ruler, beside the commentary's pulley, traveller's water, and royal-water wordplay.
The commentary treats water as the support of life and rule; David refuses to drink the water because it represents the blood of men who risked their lives to fetch it.
The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Daniel sees the court sit and books open, giving an apocalyptic court scene for divine judgment.

basis: a human-like figure approaches the Ancient of Days
note: The commentary calls God the sovereign of the judgment day; Daniel sees one like a son of man come before the Ancient of Days in the heavenly court.
The commentary calls God mālik and Lord of all worlds; Daniel’s human-like figure receives dominion and a kingdom served by all peoples and nations.
The commentary follows rain into soil and plants; Deuteronomy contrasts a land that drinks rain from heaven with Egypt’s irrigation, making rainfall the land’s source of fertility.
The promised land drinks water from rain of the heavens, directly holding together sky, rain, ground, and dependence that the commentary develops under the Arabic sky/cloud naming.

The commentary's source label س م و develops sky, cloud, rain, and plant under samāʾ. Hebrew šāmayim in this verse is a cognate sky term, but the verse keeps heaven and its rain distinct while making the land drink the rain; that difference is informative rather than evidence for identical usage.
The commentary traces rain to vegetation and provision; Deuteronomy promises rain at its proper season so grain, wine, and oil can grow.

The rain in its season yields grain, wine, oil, and grass for livestock. This is a close biblical analogue to the commentary's sequence from poured water to human food, animal provision, and livelihood.

basis: blessing or curse set before the people
note: The commentary distinguishes those granted favor from those under wrath or astray; Deuteronomy explicitly sets blessing and curse before Israel in the same chapter that ties rain to obedience and harvest.
The commentary asks for the path of those given favor; Deuteronomy says blessing follows listening to the LORD’s commandments.
The commentary asks not to follow the straying path; Deuteronomy names a curse for disobeying and turning aside to other gods.

basis: life and good set against death and evil
note: The commentary asks for the straight path and distinguishes its people from those who stray; Moses places life and good before Israel alongside death and evil.
The commentary seeks the way of those granted favor, not the way of wrath; Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and sets life and death, blessing and curse before the people.

basis: hold fast to God, who is life
note: The commentary asks to be guided on a path that sustains life; Deuteronomy says to love the LORD, listen to his voice, and hold fast to him because he is the people’s life.
The commentary says rain writes its mark in green growth and asks for guidance; Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew that fall on tender grass, making the same image a vehicle for instruction.

The commentary labels its cloud and tender-plant forms from R-B-B; Deuteronomy uses Hebrew revivim for showers falling on tender grass, a plausible cognate cluster whose exact lexical relationship should be checked in the Hebrew text.

basis: springs and streams in good land
note: The commentary pairs the traveler’s road with water and treats water as the support of livelihood; Deuteronomy describes a land of brooks, springs, and deep waters that sustains its inhabitants.

The good land is defined by brooks, fountains, and depths issuing in valley and hill. It complements the commentary's deep water-filled well and its concern that a water source might withdraw underground.

basis: full clouds empty rain on earth
note: When clouds are full, they pour rain on the earth. The compact image answers the commentary's layered cloud, its accumulated moisture, and the eventual transfer of gathered water to the ground.

The waters at Marah are made sweet so the people can drink. It offers a specific biblical analogue to the commentary's distinction of abundant water that can be called sweet and water that repairs a people's condition.

Israel reaches Elim, with twelve water springs and seventy palms, and camps by the water. This joins a travelling people, a water source, and flourishing vegetation in the concrete way the commentary joins road, well, and growing ground.
The commentary links the road with the traveler’s need for water; Exodus says Israel travels through the wilderness and has no water to drink, making thirst an immediate danger of the route.
The commentary treats water as what keeps a traveler’s affairs standing; in the wilderness God brings water from the rock at Horeb for the people to drink.
Water comes from the struck rock so that the people may drink. This gives a wilderness counterpart to the commentary's claim that water is what keeps communal and travelling life standing.
The commentary sends Musa on a road to Midian and then to its water; Exodus 2:15 sends fleeing Moses to Midian, where he sits by a well, supplying the same journey-to-well opening.
Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well, the direct narrative setting behind the commentary's Musa who reaches the water of Midian while seeking a way on his journey.
The commentary identifies two women unable to water their herds; Exodus 2:16 has seven daughters come to draw water and fill the troughs, giving the shared well scene its Israelite form.

The verse gives the precise well-side tableau developed beside Qur'an 28:23: Midian's priest has daughters who draw water and fill troughs to water their flock; Exodus says seven where the Qur'anic scene has two.
The commentary says Musa waters the women’s flocks; Exodus 2:17 has Moses rise, defend the daughters from shepherds, and water their flock.

basis: who makes room at the well
note: The commentary says the women wait for shepherds to leave and Musa then waters them; Exodus has Moses drive the shepherds off himself, shifting the aid from waiting and serving to direct intervention.

basis: Moses aids women and waters flock
note: Exodus makes Moses drive off the hostile shepherds and personally water the flock. It is the close counterpart to the commentary's two women who cannot water until the shepherds leave and are then helped by Musa.
The commentary’s scene ends with Musa watering two women’s flocks; Exodus 2:19 has the daughters report that an Egyptian rescued them and drew water for them and their flock.
The commentary says rain improves people’s state and benefits them; Ezekiel promises showers of blessing, making rain a direct sign of restored divine care.
The commentary links rain, renewed earth, and raising the dead; Ezekiel’s breath enters the bones, they live, and stand on their feet as a vast assembly.
The commentary’s rain revives dead earth and points toward resurrection; Ezekiel is told to promise breath to dry bones so that they will live.
The commentary’s ribba is a plant that does not wither in summer; Ezekiel’s trees beside the river bear fruit every month and keep leaves that do not wither.

Trees beside the river bear fruit continually and their leaves do not wither because their water comes from the sanctuary. It directly amplifies the commentary's enduring green plant and abundant sustaining water.

Where the temple river goes, every living creature lives and the water becomes fresh. It supplies a concentrated account of water's restorative, life-making work behind the commentary's full, sweet, beneficial water.

The commentary says the first rain marks soil with green growth and distinguishes favored from rejected paths; Ezekiel orders a mark on the foreheads of those who grieve, so they are distinguished when judgment falls.

The earth is commanded to sprout grass, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees. Read after the gathered-water scene of Genesis 1:9, its own contribution is the created vegetation that corresponds to the commentary's ground marked and grown green.

The commentary labels bism with S-M-W and develops Arabic sama for cloud, rain, and plant; Genesis uses the related Hebrew shamayim for the heavens, retaining the sky sense while the commentary’s Arabic examples extend it to what falls and grows.

The waters below the sky are gathered into one place so that dry ground appears. It is a foundational counterpart to the commentary's claim that abundant water is named for its gathering and to its distinction between water above and water held below.

basis: shade and rest in the day’s heat
note: The commentary has Musa withdraw to shade after watering the women; Genesis places Abraham at his tent entrance under the oaks in the heat of the day, a parallel of shelter after exertion.
The commentary joins water at the well with Musa’s retreat to shade; Abraham offers water to wash his visitors’ feet and rest under a tree, bringing water and shade together in hospitality.
The commentary follows water into food and livelihood; Abraham’s visitors are offered bread after water and rest, extending the same hospitality sequence from drink to food.
The commentary links water to vegetation and livelihood; Genesis 2:10 describes a river flowing from Eden to water the garden, locating plant life beside a sustaining source.

basis: water from the ground sustains land
note: The commentary distinguishes rain from above and well water drawn from below; Genesis 2:6 pictures mist rising from the ground to water the soil before cultivated growth.

A water source rising from the earth waters the whole ground before rain is mentioned. Because the Hebrew term's exact physical sense is debated, it is a cautious companion to the commentary's two routes of water: sky-rain and water drawn from below.

basis: water runs out in the wilderness
note: The commentary asks who can bring running water when a person’s supply sinks away; Hagar’s water skin is empty in the wilderness, making thirst on a journey concrete.
The commentary asks who supplies water when it disappears; God opens Hagar’s eyes to a well, and she draws water for the child, a direct scene of provision after water runs out.
When Hagar's water is gone in the wilderness, God opens her eyes to a well. It is a concrete companion to the commentary's traveller whose survival and affairs depend on water being found or brought.

basis: traveler and camels at a well
note: The commentary makes a road traveler’s water and a well central; Abraham’s servant reaches a town well with camels and waits there as women come to draw water.

basis: camels at well at drawing time
note: Abraham's servant stops with camels at a well at the time women come to draw water. It supplies the practical journey-and-well setting behind the commentary's water carried by a traveller.

basis: prayer for success at the well
note: After Musa waters the women, the commentary quotes his prayer for whatever good God sends; Abraham’s servant prays at the well for success, making a water encounter the setting for a request for divine direction.

basis: women draw water at the spring
note: The commentary centers women who come to a water source with flocks; the servant in Genesis stands by the spring as the city’s daughters come out to draw water.

basis: water for a stranger and his animals
note: The commentary’s Musa waters women’s flocks; Rebekah gives Abraham’s servant a drink and then draws for his camels, closely joining stranger, well, and animal water.
Rebekah draws until the camels have drunk. Her labour at the well gives another concrete biblical instance of water as the support of travellers and animals.
Isaac's servants dig in a valley and find a well described as living water. Its fresh, discovered source closely meets the commentary's deep, full well and its concern for sweet, abundant water.
The commentary moves from rain to green land and food; Isaac’s blessing asks for dew from heaven, fatness of earth, and abundant grain and wine.

basis: Jacob opens the well and waters a flock
note: The commentary’s Musa waters women’s flocks at a well; Jacob moves the stone from the well’s mouth and waters Rachel’s flock, another well-side meeting involving a woman and animal water.

basis: traveller rolls well stone and waters flock
note: The travelling Jacob rolls the covering stone from the well's mouth and waters Laban's flock. It joins road, well mechanism, and life-giving water in the way the commentary joins the straight path to the water that sustains a traveller.

The commentary describes the mouth of a well and its beam, pulley, and bucket; Jacob’s scene identifies a large stone laid over the well’s mouth, giving a distinct biblical mechanism for controlling access to well water.

The verse places three flocks at a well whose mouth is covered by a large stone, because the flocks are watered there. It supplies a biblical well-mouth structure for the commentary's beam, pulley, and watering work.

The commentary says the women wait to water until shepherds depart; Genesis has shepherds wait until all flocks gather before moving the stone and watering them, making control of access to a well part of the scene.

The commentary says Yusuf’s brothers propose the pit so a passing traveler may take him; Reuben instead proposes the pit to keep the brothers from killing Joseph, a shared rescue-through-the-pit plan with a changed rationale.

The commentary describes Yusuf thrown into the dark bottom of a well before travelers arrive; Genesis has Joseph put into an empty cistern, matching the pit while withholding the Qur’anic water-drawing detail.
The commentary’s next Yusuf scene has a bucket lowered to draw water and a boy discovered; Genesis explicitly says Joseph’s cistern was empty, making the means of discovery differ.
Genesis explicitly calls Joseph's pit empty and waterless. That sharpens the commentary's contrasting Qur'anic well scene, where a caravan's water-drawer lowers a bucket and finds the boy.

basis: caravan and the boy in the pit
note: The commentary says a caravan arrives and its water drawer finds Yusuf; Genesis has traders pass and Joseph brought up from the pit and sold to the Ishmaelites, sharing the pit-and-caravan turn.

The commentary makes the lowered water bucket the way the passing caravan finds Yusuf; Genesis has traders pull Joseph from the pit and sell him, replacing a chance discovery during water-drawing with deliberate removal and sale.

Midianite traders draw and lift Joseph from the pit and carry him away. The commentary's Qur'anic caravan likewise removes Joseph from a well, but gives the discovery to a water-carrier lowering his bucket.
God will be like dew to Israel, and Israel will blossom like the lily. This adds the secondary, non-rain moisture route by which divine beneficence makes a plant fresh and flourishing.
The commentary cites rain as a sign of the earth’s revival and connects rain to raising the dead; Hosea promises that God will revive Israel and raise it up on the third day.
The commentary makes rain a sign of divine benefit and renewal; Hosea compares God’s coming to dawn and to rain that waters the earth, giving the rain a covenantal and restorative meaning.
God's coming is compared to rain and to the latter rain watering the earth. It directly supplies the rain-as-divine-mercy reading that the commentary develops around rahmet and revived ground.
Joyful drawing from wells becomes the image of salvation. The verse gives a scriptural way in which the literal action central to the commentary's pulley and well bears a second, saving sense.
YHWH guards the vineyard and waters it continually. It supplies the direct divine-cultivator sense that the commentary hears in Rab as the one associated with plant growth.
The commentary asks God to guide people on a straight road; Isaiah promises a voice behind the listener saying “this is the way, walk in it,” an explicit divine direction for the traveler.
The commentary joins the straight road to rain-fed growth and food; immediately after Isaiah’s way instruction, God sends rain for the seed sown in the ground and makes the harvest abundant.

basis: rain for seed, rich bread, livestock
note: Rain is given for the seed sown in the ground, producing abundant bread and pasture for livestock. This directly meets the commentary's water, food, animals, and sustaining livelihood.

basis: wind shelter, dry-land stream, and shade
note: The commentary brings wind, water, and Musa’s shade together; Isaiah describes a refuge from wind and storm, streams in dry land, and shade from a great rock in a weary land.

basis: sowing by waters with ox and donkey
note: The blessed sow beside all waters and let ox and donkey range out. It joins water, cultivation, and working animals, the same practical provision sequence that the commentary traces from rain to food and livestock.
The commentary places road travel, thirst, and water together; Isaiah says waters break out in the wilderness and streams in the desert, turning the barren route into a place of life.

basis: waters in wilderness, streams in desert
note: Waters break out in the wilderness and streams in the desert. The verse makes the life-restoring turn from dryness to water that the commentary associates with rain, mercy, and fresh life.

The commentary’s sirat is a path the traveler walks with water at hand; Isaiah 35:8 describes a highway called the Holy Way for the redeemed, pairing a marked route with the wilderness water of the same restoration scene.
The commentary pairs the straight path with travel and water in the wilderness; Isaiah calls for a highway to be made straight in the desert for God.

basis: needy seek water and find none
note: The poor and needy seek water with their tongues parched, and God answers them. It is a direct companion to the commentary's question of who can bring water when a community's water has gone down.

basis: rivers, fountains, pools on dry land
note: God opens rivers and fountains and turns wilderness into pools and dry ground into springs. This is a direct biblical counterpart to both the commentary's well-water and its fear that water may sink out of reach.
The commentary’s rain repairs people’s condition and benefits them; Isaiah promises water for thirsty land and streams on dry ground, followed by God’s spirit on the people.

Water is poured on thirsty land and streams on dry ground. It directly parallels the commentary's rain sent to barren earth, while its following spiritual application makes the literal image more than a weather report.
The commentary says the first rain marks earth with plants; Isaiah pictures descendants springing up like grass and willows beside flowing water.

The heavens rain and the earth opens to sprout salvation and righteousness. It recasts the commentary's rain-and-growing-earth image as an ethical and saving figure rather than a purely agricultural one.
The commentary’s straight road includes water for the traveler; Isaiah says the compassionate guide leads the redeemed beside springs, where they do not hunger or thirst.

The compassionate guide leads the hungry and thirsty to springs of water. Its explicit joining of guidance, a way, and water is a strong companion to the commentary's straight path beside the sustaining well.

basis: sheep gone astray from their way
note: The commentary asks not to follow those who stray and elsewhere describes flocks at the well; Isaiah says all sheep have gone astray, each turning to its own way, joining animal wandering to the path language.
The thirsty are invited to come to water without payment. Its invitation turns the commentary's traveller's necessary water into a public gift available to those in need.
The commentary’s first rain marks soil with vegetation and then becomes food; Isaiah says rain and snow water the earth, make it bud, and provide seed and bread.

basis: rain’s work and the effective word
note: The commentary describes rain as a mark written into the earth and asks for guidance; Isaiah compares the word from God’s mouth to rain that does not return before accomplishing its purpose.
The commentary joins a request for the straight path to water that sustains life; Isaiah says the LORD will guide continually and make the faithful like a watered garden and an unfailing spring.

God continually guides, satisfies the parched person, and makes that person like a watered garden and an unfailing spring. It closely joins the commentary's guidance, fresh life, and never-failing water.

basis: Arabic q-w-m and Hebrew qwm restore
note: The commentary's ق و م label names the pulley and what makes an affair stand. Hebrew qwm in this verse describes raising up and restoring enduring foundations; beside the watered-garden guidance of verse 11, it supplies a cognate support-and-restoration sense without claiming a well in Isaiah 58:12.

basis: wind, clouds, and rain in sequence
note: The commentary says winds move and spread clouds before rain; Jeremiah says God makes clouds rise, flashes lightning for rain, and brings wind from storehouses.

Jeremiah asks whether foreign gods or the heavens can give showers, and confesses that YHWH made all these things. This makes rain a dependent gift of the creator, closely matching the commentary's rain as mercy and benefit rather than autonomous weather.

The nobles send servants for water, but cisterns have none and the vessels return empty. Its social consequence of missing water is a direct counterpart to the commentary's question of who can bring water when a community's source has withdrawn.
The commentary distinguishes those given favor from those under wrath or astray; Jeremiah sets the blessed person who trusts the LORD against the dry shrub of the preceding verse.
The commentary’s tender plant does not wither in summer; Jeremiah’s tree beside water is unafraid of heat, keeps green leaves, and does not stop bearing fruit.

basis: tree by water stays green in drought
note: The water-side tree has green leaves and does not cease bearing fruit in drought. Its drought-resistant freshness is a particularly close counterpart to the commentary's summer-unwithered ribbe plant.
The commentary asks who can bring running water when it sinks away; Jeremiah calls God the fountain of living waters and condemns people who abandon it for cracked cisterns that cannot hold water.

The people abandon a fountain of living water for cracked cisterns that cannot retain water. It offers a negative well-and-storage counterpart to the commentary's gathered water and the structural devices at a well's mouth.

The restored people receive grain, wine, oil, flock, and herd, and their life becomes like a watered garden. This is the necessary agricultural continuation of the watercourse-and-straight-way image in Jeremiah 31:9 already relevant to the commentary.

God leads the returning people to watercourses on a straight path where they do not stumble. This is an unusually exact meeting of the commentary's dosdoğru yol with water that makes the journey possible.

basis: tree renewal beside the question of human life
note: The commentary connects revived earth with the raising of the dead; Job asks whether a human who dies will live again after describing a tree renewed by water.
The commentary describes tender growth that survives summer and rain that revives the earth; Job says a felled tree still has hope of sprouting again.

basis: scent of water renews the tree
note: The commentary says rain marks soil with green growth; Job’s tree buds and puts forth branches at the scent of water, making renewed vegetation a sign of life after apparent death.
The commentary describes clouds that carry water and grow plants; Job says God draws up drops of water and distills rain from the mist.
Job describes God drawing up drops of water and distilling them as rain. It offers a precise account of the water-to-cloud-to-rain process behind the commentary's layered, plant-growing cloud.
The commentary develops the cloud as a layered bearer of rain; Job says clouds pour down water upon humankind.
The skies pour water down abundantly on humankind. This gives a direct counterpart to the commentary's gathering of abundant water and rain as public benefit.
The thick cloud is loaded with moisture and then spread abroad. Its particular image of a moisture-bearing cloud parallels the commentary's layered cloud and the wet wind associated with it.
The commentary presents rain as what restores soil and makes it useful; Job asks who sends rain on land where no person lives, watering the wilderness for growth.
The commentary follows rain into green growth and provision; Joel promises early and late rains as part of restoration, tying weather to renewed harvest.
The rain is given in its proper season, including the early and latter rains. It provides a biblical seasonal setting for the commentary's first rain that marks the earth with vegetation.
The commentary traces water toward food; Joel’s restoration scene has threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing after the rains.
The commentary’s cloud and rain enlarge the earth with plant growth; Leviticus promises seasonal rain followed by a land that yields produce and trees that bear fruit.
Seasonal rain makes the land yield produce and trees bear fruit. It directly supplies the rain-to-growing-earth sequence through which the commentary hears the growing Rab and the rain-marked ground.

basis: water gushes from the rock again
note: The commentary presents water as life-sustaining provision; in a second wilderness account Moses strikes the rock and water gushes out for the congregation and their animals.

Israel asks to travel on the king's highway while promising not to drink from field, vineyard, or well. The verse unusually binds road, traveller, well water, and king in one practical scene, directly meeting the commentary's straight path and water-as-royal-support imagery.
The commentary joins journey, well, and water for people and flocks; at Beer God tells Moses to gather the people and promises to give them water.

At Beer, God commands that the people be gathered so that he may give them water. The collective provisioning clarifies why the commentary treats a well as the support of an affair rather than a private possession.
The commentary carefully develops the well’s mouth and the apparatus for drawing water; Israel sings to the well, “Spring up,” making a well itself the focus of a public water song.

Israel answers the provision of water with the command to the well to spring up and with a song. The liturgical address makes the well itself a source of communal life, matching the commentary's concentrated water imagery.
The commentary says water is the support and “king” of communal affairs; Numbers says princes and nobles dug this well with their staffs, tying water access to leaders’ work.

basis: well dug by nobles with staffs
note: The well is dug by princes and hollowed by nobles with their staffs. As the necessary continuation of the well-song, it makes rulership and a constructed water source meet, closely accompanying the commentary's waters called rulers and its beam-and-pulley well mouth.

basis: Hebrew shem, name placed on people
note: The commentary labels bism with a name-related source and then links it to wasm, a mark made by first rain; Numbers says the priests put God’s name upon Israel and God blesses them, joining name, marking, and benefit.

A person who boasts of a false gift is like clouds and wind with no rain. This negative weather image precisely defines the loss implicit in the commentary's productive cloud: visible cloud and wind do not suffice unless water reaches the earth.

By divine knowledge the depths break open and the skies drip dew. It is a compact biblical pairing of water from below with moisture from above, closely matching the commentary's well-water and heaven-rain as two routes of water.
The commentary’s central request is guidance on the straight path; Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one’s ways results in God making the paths straight.

basis: cistern and own well as ethical figure
note: The proverb commands drinking from one's own cistern and well. It takes the literal infrastructure central to the commentary and makes its contained water an ethical image of faithful, rightly bounded household life.

basis: tree beside streams, leaf does not wither
note: The commentary’s ribba is a tender plant said not to wither in summer; Psalm 1’s tree by streams bears fruit and keeps its leaf, joining steady water to enduring growth.

basis: tree by water, leaf does not wither
note: The tree planted by channels of water bears fruit and does not wither. It is the closest biblical image for the commentary's tender plant that remains fresh even through summer.

The commentary pairs the straight path with the Day of Judgment and distinguishes graced people from those under wrath; Psalm 1 says the wicked will not stand in judgment or in the righteous assembly.

The commentary labels mustaqim from Q-W-M and says water is what makes affairs stand; Psalm 1 uses Hebrew yaqumu for sinners who will not stand in judgment, connecting uprightness with the judgment scene.

basis: the righteous way and the perishing way
note: The commentary asks for the path of the favored rather than those who stray; Psalm 1 says the LORD knows the way of the righteous while the wicked way perishes.
The commentary connects hamd with rain and the earth’s fertility; Psalm 104 begins in praise and then describes God’s care of clouds, mountains, plants, and food.
The commentary describes layered clouds and rain that grows plants; Psalm 104 says God waters the mountains from the upper chambers and satisfies the earth with fruit.
God waters the mountains from his upper chambers, and the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his work. It is a close scriptural formulation of heavenly water sustaining terrestrial growth.
The commentary follows rain into tender plants and fields; Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for people to cultivate.

basis: grass and plants grow from water
note: The same hymn says God causes grass to grow for cattle and plants for human cultivation. It supplies the food-and-livestock outcome that the commentary connects to rain and provision.

basis: food and drink from the earth
note: The commentary links water to livelihood and food; Psalm 104 names wine, oil, and bread as gifts that gladden, nourish, and strengthen human life.
The commentary says rain restores soil and makes it fruitful; Psalm 107 says God turns wilderness into a pool and parched land into springs.

basis: desert turned to pools and springs
note: God turns desert into a pool and parched ground into water springs. The reversal makes a concrete companion to rain repairing a people's condition and to water being drawn from otherwise dry ground.
The commentary moves from water to livelihood; Psalm 107 says God settles hungry people there and they establish a city to live in.
The commentary follows rain into plants and food; Psalm 107 describes sowing fields, planting vineyards, and obtaining a fruitful yield.
The commentary says rain improves people’s condition and feeds animals; Psalm 107 says God blesses the people so they multiply and their livestock increase.
The commentary’s N-ʿ-M family describes life’s beauty and freshness; Psalm 133 calls shared life good and pleasant with Hebrew na'im, a cognate use centered on what is delightful.

basis: wind and rain from God’s storehouses
note: The commentary pairs wind, heavy cloud, and rainfall; Psalm 135 gives the same cluster as God’s work, bringing clouds, lightning for rain, and winds from storehouses.
The commentary asks for the straight way; the psalm asks God’s good Spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, a specific guidance formula.
The commentary places hamd beside rain and mercy; Psalm 147’s call to sing with thanksgiving leads directly into its account of clouds, rain, grass, and animal food.

basis: cloud, rain, and grass in one verse
note: The commentary links clouds and moisture to plant growth; Psalm 147 says God covers the heavens with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the hills.
God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on hills. Its exact three-part image is especially close to the commentary's cloud, rain, and plant meeting.
The commentary follows rain into pasture and names water as the support of affairs; Psalm 147 says God gives food to beasts and to the young ravens that cry.

The commentary explicitly ties أَنْعَمْتَ and n-ʿ-m to freshness and beneficent support. Hebrew neʿimot, a cognate form here, accompanies the path of life and enduring delight; it gives a linguistic and contextual companion to the commentary's path plus life-giving blessing.

The commentary labels hamd from Ḥ-M-D and says the earth is pleasing to inhabit or pasture; Psalm 19 calls the teaching desirable, a possible cognate that preserves a pleasing/desirable sense without equating it with praise.
The commentary’s well scene moves from watering to shade, and its rain grows plants; the shepherd leads the speaker to green pasture and still water, portraying care as food and water on a journey.

basis: green pasture and waters of rest
note: The shepherd makes the speaker rest in green pastures and leads beside waters of rest. It combines the commentary's growing ground, water, guidance, and wayfarer in one pastoral line.
The commentary asks for the straight path and says water keeps the traveler’s affairs upright; the shepherd restores the soul and leads by paths of righteousness.
The commentary places Musa in shade after watering the women; the psalm describes walking through the shadowed valley under the shepherd’s protection.
The commentary extends rain and water into food for people and animals; the shepherd prepares a table and provides an overflowing cup, completing its picture of provision along the way.

basis: prayer to be led in God’s truth
note: The commentary’s central petition is “guide us” on a straight path; David asks God to lead him in truth and teach him, a close prayer-form parallel.
The commentary grounds guidance in divine favor and benefit; the psalm asks God to remember compassion and steadfast love, linking direction to mercy.

The verse calls YHWH melekh, a cognate of the commentary's م ل ك / mālik label, while placing him over the flood. It gives a substantive Hebrew king-and-water meeting, not merely a shared root, beside the commentary's water as what holds an affair together.
The commentary says water is the support by which affairs stand; Psalm 46’s river gladdens God’s city, where God’s presence keeps it from being moved.

The commentary labels Qur’anic mālik from M-L-K and calls water “our kings”; Psalm 47 uses the cognate Hebrew melek for God as king over all earth, showing the sovereignty sense beyond the water metaphor.
The commentary links rain with mercy and the revival of soil; Psalm 65 says God visits and waters the earth, filling the divine river and preparing grain.
God waters furrows, softens earth with showers, and blesses its growth. This particularly matches the commentary's first rain writing vegetation into the ground and the cloud that grows plants.

basis: showers soften furrows and bless growth
note: The commentary traces the first rain into green plants and provision; Psalm 65 pictures showers softening the furrows and blessing the growth of the earth.
The commentary says rain leaves a green mark on the soil and pairs water with the straight path; Psalm 65 says God’s tracks drip with abundance as the year is crowned with goodness.
The commentary takes rain through soil to plants and food; Psalm 65 ends with pastures, hills, and valleys clothed in flocks and grain.
The commentary cites rain, mercy, and hamd together in Qur’an 42:28; Psalm 65 opens with praise to God and then describes God watering the earth and making it fruitful.

basis: grace and blessing for the people
note: The commentary connects hamd with rain and mercy; Psalm 67 asks God to be gracious and bless the people before describing the earth’s yield and the nations’ praise.
The commentary traces rain to plants and food; Psalm 67 says the earth has yielded its increase and asks God to bless the people.
The commentary names the Lord of all worlds and invokes praise; Psalm 67 ends with all the ends of the earth fearing God after the earth’s harvest.
The commentary calls God mālik on the Day of Judgment and says water is “our king”; Psalm 72 asks that the king judge the people with righteousness and the poor with justice.

basis: rain on cut grass under the king
note: The commentary joins the kingly water image to rain-fed growth; Psalm 72 compares the king’s reign to rain falling on mown grass and showers watering the earth.

basis: water from the deep in the wilderness
note: The commentary explains that water holds up the traveler’s affairs; Psalm 78 recalls God splitting rocks in the wilderness and giving drink as from the deep.
The commentary moves between the deep well and water that sustains life; Psalm 78 says streams came from the rock and ran like rivers.

basis: water and food on the journey
note: The commentary traces water toward food and livelihood; Psalm 78 recalls water gushing from the rock and immediately asks whether God can also provide bread and meat.

basis: Baca valley made a spring by rain
note: Those crossing the Valley of Baca make it a place of springs, and early rain covers it with blessings. The transforming rain-and-spring image supplies a pilgrimage-scale companion to the commentary's path that cannot be separated from water.
The commentary names God as ruler of the Day of Judgment and Lord of the worlds; Psalm 96 says the LORD reigns and judges the peoples with equity.

basis: God comes to judge the earth
note: The commentary calls God the Owner of the Day of Judgment; Psalm 96 says God comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with faithfulness.

basis: garden fountain and well of living water
note: The beloved is called a garden fountain, a well of living waters, and streams flowing from Lebanon. Its gathered garden, well, freshness, and flow make it a particularly close biblical companion to the commentary's full well and unfading vegetation.

basis: ask for rain in its season
note: The commentary’s imagery treats rain as provision from God; Zechariah explicitly tells people to ask the LORD for rain at the time of spring rain.

basis: spring rain, storm clouds, field plants
note: God makes storm clouds, gives rain showers, and provides vegetation in every field. The verse has the same cloud-rain-plant sequence developed in the commentary.

basis: living waters in summer and winter
note: Living waters flow in both summer and winter. Its year-round flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's fresh plant that does not fade in summer and its well of plentiful water.
